slides.title: 7.2.1 Implementing Separate Chaining
keyPoints: In separate chaining, each bucket owns a vector of key/value pairs.
Put scans that bucket to update an existing key or appends a new pair.
Get scans for equality, and erase removes the matching pair.
The outer table owns all buckets and their contained values.
slides.narration: In Book III, Chapter 7, treat 7.2.1 Implementing Separate Chaining as an algorithmic claim. In separate chaining, each bucket owns a vector of key/value pairs. Put scans that bucket to update an existing key or appends a new pair. Get scans for equality, and erase removes the matching pair. The outer table owns all buckets and their contained values. Lookup cost depends on the bucket length; insertion can also allocate as a bucket grows. This representation uses vectors rather than linked nodes, demonstrating that chaining is an abstract collision strategy, not a requirement for one node layout. A missing key returns an empty optional, while storing a value zero remains unambiguous. At a graduate level, the answer is never just that the code ran. slides.title: Failure clinic — Deletion made an unrelated key disappear
keyPoints: A lookup works until another colliding key is erased.
Inspect the deleted slot’s state.
Replacing occupied with empty instead of tombstone breaks the proof that search may stop at an empty slot.
The repair is to preserve probe continuity, not to scan every table slot unconditionally and abandon the intended.
slides.narration: In Book III, Chapter 7, treat Failure clinic — Deletion made an unrelated key disappear as an algorithmic claim. A lookup works until another colliding key is erased. Inspect the deleted slot’s state. Replacing occupied with empty instead of tombstone breaks the proof that search may stop at an empty slot. The repair is to preserve probe continuity, not to scan every table slot unconditionally and abandon the intended mechanism. An update appears correct, but a subsequent erase reveals an older value for the same key. That symptom suggests duplicate insertion at a tombstone before checking for an existing later key. Preserve the first reusable slot while continuing the equality search. The new value must replace the existing entry, not create a competing one. At a graduate level, the answer is never just that the code ran.
